messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: lavaan error
parts:
Pat--
     Another dependent variable would give the factor three "indicators," sure, and that would establish identification independent of everything else. But two indicators is enough for identification as long as the factor is correlated with something else, as this factor obviously is. If the factor were *not* correlated, then all model-implied covariances for the factor's indicators and all other observed variables would become 0, and so could not be used to estimate parameters for the factor. But since the factor correlates with other things, you *can* use those elements of the covariance matrix to solve for more model parameters.
     Take a simple model with two factors and two indicators each. Typically, that will mean 9 free parameters (4 loadings, 4 observed variable residual variances, 1 factor correlation--if you standardize the factors), but the covariance matrix will have 4*(4-1)/2 = 10 unique elements. But if the two factors are uncorrelated, then all of the cross-covariances between indicators of different factors in the model-implied covariance matrix will include the 0 factor covariance in their formulas, and so will have 0 values overall, and can't be used to solve for other model parameters. So then you really have only 6 elements of the covariance matrix for estimating the 8 other parameters (beside the factor correlation).

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: lavaan error
parts: PA2 has two indicators, no other variables downstream from it, and no other constraints. Doesn't that fail the structural identification rules?

2-indicator factors with different free factor loadings can be identified when the factor covaries substantially with at least one other factor (which can also have 2 indicators with free loadings).  The information that identifies differences in factor loadings within the 2-indicator factor is obtained from the differences in how indicators from one factor correlate with indicators from the other.  The mathematical proof is here:

http://ww.w.statpower.net/Steiger%20Biblio/Steiger02.PDF

But as Ed said, whether that is empirically identified is entirely dependent on how much information there is in the correlations between indicators of different factors.  When they are not substantial, then the factor correlation will approach zero, and the model will not be identified (regardless of N).  I attached some slides I put together recently to demonstrate this with simulated data (and how Heywood cases can be caused by sampling error alone).  

Silvia, can you post your model-implied latent (residual and marginal) covariance matrices?

lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv") # marginal
lavInspect(fit, "est")$psi # residual
## standardized
lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv") # marginal
lavInspect(fit, "std")$psi # residual

Just curious where the Heywood case is popping up.  Since your time-2 factors are autoregressed on Time 1, I am surprised your 2-indicator factor is identified at Time 2 because I expect after conditioning on Time 1 (where the variables were also allowed to correlate), there is not much reason left for their Time-2 residuals to correlate very high.  But of course you have more information for empirical identification, since one of the factors has 5 indicators rather than 2.

I notice you have an _r suffix on one indicator at Time 2 that is not there at Time 1.  If your 2 indicators are not in the same direction, then that would imply their shared variance (i.e., covariance) is negative.   See the attached slides for an example.
